prompt: Quitanda moves its orders database to RDS. A report added on Monday reads the whole `orders` table every minute and the CPU sits at 95%. Who adds the missing index?
hint: Which column of the table holds indexes?

choices.text: RDS, once its metrics show the CPU high for long enough
choices.why: RDS reports the CPU; it never changes a schema, and an index is part of the schema.

choices.text: Quitanda: indexes stay with whoever owns the schema
choices.why: Right. Managed moves the operational work, and the schema, the queries and the indexes stay where they were.

choices.text: AWS Support, as part of the managed service
choices.why: Nothing in the managed list touches what is inside the database.

choices.text: Nobody; the fix is a larger instance class
choices.why: A bigger instance is the expensive way to hide a missing index, and the report still reads the whole table.

prompt: An application on Quitanda's old server used a PostgreSQL extension compiled there by hand. What happens when the database moves to RDS?
hint: Think about what the master user is, and whether there is a shell.

choices.text: It is copied across with the data by the migration
choices.why: A dump carries the data and the schema, not the compiled library the extension needs on the server.

choices.text: The master user installs it with `CREATE EXTENSION`
choices.why: Only extensions on RDS's list can be created; the master user is in `rds_superuser`, not a real superuser.

choices.text: It cannot be used unless RDS lists it
choices.why: Right. No shell, no file system, and extensions only from the allowed list.

choices.text: You log in over SSH and compile it again
choices.why: An RDS instance offers no login to its operating system at all.

prompt: Which of these does RDS do for you? Choose all that apply.
hint: The left column is the work that is the same for every database.

choices.text: Apply operating system patches to the database server
choices.why: Yes; you never see that operating system.

choices.text: Take automated backups and keep them for the retention you set
choices.why: Yes, up to 35 days; lesson 7 restores from them.

choices.text: Rewrite a query that reads a million rows to return ten
choices.why: Queries are the application's, on RDS as anywhere.

choices.text: Choose how many connections the application opens
choices.why: RDS sets a limit; what opens connections, and how many, is the application's design.

choices.text: Replace the hardware when it fails
choices.why: Yes; the machine is AWS's.

prompt: A company wants Oracle Enterprise Edition on RDS and holds no Oracle licence. What can it do?
hint: Look at the licence column for `oracle-ee`.

choices.text: Choose `license-included`, and pay Oracle's share inside the hourly price, as with SQL Server
choices.why: That works for Standard Edition 2 and for SQL Server; Enterprise Edition is offered only as bring your own.

choices.text: Get one from the vendor first, or run SE2 with the price covering it
choices.why: Right. EE is bring-your-own only; SE2 can come with the licence in the price.

choices.text: Nothing: Oracle does not run on RDS
choices.why: Oracle is one of the five engines; the question is who pays for the licence.

choices.text: Use Aurora, which runs Oracle with no licence
choices.why: Aurora speaks PostgreSQL or MySQL, never Oracle.

prompt: In moto, an instance created without `--engine-version` came back as PostgreSQL 9.3.3. A colleague concludes RDS still creates 9.3 by default. What is wrong with that?
hint: Whose default answered?

choices.text: Nothing; 9.3 is what RDS picks when no version is given
choices.why: AWS picks its current default version; 9.3 is long gone from RDS.

choices.text: 9.3.3 is a minor version, and RDS only reports major ones
choices.why: RDS reports the full version; the problem is whose default it is.

choices.text: It is moto's old default; AWS picks its current one
choices.why: Right. Name the version in every command so the result does not depend on who answered.

choices.text: The default changes with the instance class
choices.why: The class decides the machine, not the engine version.

prompt: Match each `--engine` value to its licence on RDS.
hint: One of them is not open source and has its licence in the hourly price.

pairs.right: Only a licence you already hold

right_distractors: Free for the first year, then included

prompt: In moto, `create-db-instance` answers `available` on the same second, with an endpoint on port 5432. What is behind that endpoint?
hint: What did moto store?

choices.text: A PostgreSQL server that moto started in the background
choices.why: moto starts no engine; the record has a status and an address and nothing listens.

choices.text: Nothing: a record with a name nobody's DNS holds
choices.why: Right. On AWS the same instance would take minutes to reach `available`, because a real machine starts.

choices.text: A read-only copy of a sample database
choices.why: moto ships no database at all.

choices.text: The real RDS endpoint, reached through moto as a proxy
choices.why: moto never talks to AWS; the lab runs with no account.

prompt: Quitanda's instance lives in one zone. Why does its DB subnet group name subnets in two?
hint: Think about lesson 7.

choices.text: AWS requires two zones, and the second is where a Multi-AZ standby would go
choices.why: Right. The room for the standby is booked when the group is made.

choices.text: The instance is split across both and reads from either
choices.why: A Single-AZ instance runs in one zone, on one volume.

choices.text: Each zone holds half of the 100 GiB volume
choices.why: The volume is in the instance's zone; nothing is halved.

choices.text: moto refuses a group with one subnet
choices.why: The two-zone rule is AWS's, documented; moto checks far less.

prompt: Why does the lesson create the instance with `--manage-master-user-password` rather than `--master-user-password`?
hint: Where does a password typed on a command line end up?

choices.text: It makes the instance start faster
choices.why: It changes where the secret lives, not how long the instance takes.

choices.text: moto refuses a typed password
choices.why: moto accepts either, even a password AWS would refuse as too short.

choices.text: A typed password is stored in plain text inside the instance
choices.why: Either way the engine stores a hash; the leak is on your side of the command.

choices.text: The password goes to Secrets Manager and never into history
choices.why: Right. RDS generates and rotates it, and the application reads it with a role; nobody types it.

prompt: moto created a `db.banana.huge` without complaint. What does that tell you about a script that creates instances and passes against moto?
hint: What does moto check, and what does AWS check?

choices.text: Only that the requests are well formed
choices.why: Right. Whether a class exists for that engine and region is AWS's check, and moto does not make it.

choices.text: That the class exists, since moto would have refused it
choices.why: moto just accepted a class that does not exist.

choices.text: That the script will work unchanged on AWS
choices.why: A success from moto means the request was well formed, and no more.

choices.text: Nothing: moto skips validation only for test-sized classes
choices.why: There are no test-sized classes; moto checks the engine and little else.

prompt: Quitanda raises `max_connections` in its parameter group with `ApplyMethod=pending-reboot`. When does the running engine use the new value?
hint: It is a static parameter.

choices.text: At once, because the group is attached to the instance
choices.why: A static parameter is read only when the engine starts.

choices.text: At the next restart, planned or not; until then AWS marks it as waiting
choices.why: Right. So the restart is scheduled like any other downtime.

choices.text: Within five minutes, when RDS reloads the configuration of every instance using the group
choices.why: Reloading works for dynamic parameters; `max_connections` sizes memory at start.

choices.text: Never, until the instance moves to a new parameter group
choices.why: The same group takes effect at the restart; no new group is needed.

prompt: Why did the lesson create `quitanda-pg16` before the instance existed, instead of using `default.postgres16`?
hint: Can a default group be changed?

choices.text: A default group cannot be changed; switching later needs a restart
choices.why: Right. Naming its own group at creation spares the instance that restart.

choices.text: Custom groups are cheaper than the default one, which is billed per instance
choices.why: Parameter groups cost nothing either way.

choices.text: The default group belongs to another account, AWS's, and yours cannot name it
choices.why: It is in your account, and it is read-only.

choices.text: An instance without a custom group gets no parameters at all
choices.why: It gets the default group's values, which is the point of having one.

prompt: After changing a static parameter, moto shows `ParameterApplyStatus: in-sync`. What would AWS show, and why does moto differ?
hint: moto keeps no running engine.

choices.text: `in-sync` too: a parameter group is applied when it is saved
choices.why: A static parameter waits for a restart, and AWS shows that it is waiting.

choices.text: `applying`, because AWS restarts the instance on its own
choices.why: AWS never restarts for a parameter change; the restart is yours to schedule.

choices.text: `pending-reboot`, since the engine still runs the old value
choices.why: Right. moto has no engine to be out of step with, so it never shows the difference.

choices.text: An error, because static parameters cannot be changed on RDS
choices.why: They can; they take effect at the next restart.

prompt: A parameter that a running engine reads again is called dynamic; one read only at start is called ___.
hint: `max_connections` is one.

prompt: A `db.m7g.large` PostgreSQL costs 0.221 USD an hour Single-AZ, and gp3 storage 0.219 per GB-month. What does it cost in a 730-hour month with 200 GiB? Give USD to two decimal places.
hint: Instance hours times price, plus GiB times price.

prompt: In the price sheet, how does a Multi-AZ PostgreSQL `db.m7g.large` compare with the same Single-AZ instance?
hint: Compare 0.442 with 0.221, and 0.438 with 0.219.

choices.text: About 10% more, for the replication traffic
choices.why: The sheet says exactly double, for the instance and for the storage.

choices.text: Double the instance, and the same storage
choices.why: The storage doubles too: the standby has a volume of its own.

choices.text: Exactly double, instance and storage both
choices.why: Right. It is a second instance with a second volume in another zone.

choices.text: The same; the standby is free until it is used
choices.why: The standby runs every hour and is billed every hour.

prompt: A `db.m6i.large` running SQL Server Standard costs 1.087 USD an hour; a `db.m7g.large` running PostgreSQL costs 0.221. Both have 2 vCPU and 8 GiB. What is most of the difference?
hint: Look at the licence column.

choices.text: The Intel processor of the `m6i`, against Graviton
choices.why: Processor families differ by cents an hour, not by four times the price.

choices.text: Microsoft's licence, billed by the hour
choices.why: Right. The engine's licence is in the hourly price, every hour it runs.

choices.text: Storage, since SQL Server needs more of it
choices.why: Storage is billed separately per GiB; these are instance prices.

choices.text: Backups, which SQL Server takes more often
choices.why: Backups are RDS's and work the same for every engine.

prompt: Put the steps of creating Quitanda's instance in the order the lesson needs them.
hint: Each step names something the step before it made.
items: Create the VPC and two subnets in two zones
Create the DB subnet group naming the two subnets
Create the instance, naming the groups and `--manage-master-user-password`
Change a static parameter, then restart the instance

prompt: A test database will not be needed for two months. Someone stops it to save money. What happens?
hint: Two things a stopped instance does not stop.

choices.text: Nothing more is billed until it is started again
choices.why: The storage is still billed while stopped.

choices.text: It is deleted after seven days of being stopped, together with all of its backups
choices.why: RDS starts it again after seven days; it deletes nothing.

choices.text: Storage keeps being billed, and RDS starts it again on its own after seven days
choices.why: Right. For two months, a snapshot and a deletion is the cheaper way.

choices.text: The instance class is lowered to the smallest one
choices.why: Stopping changes no class; the hourly charge for the machine simply stops.

prompt: Quitanda's functions open a new connection for every request and hit `max_connections`. Which fix fits what the lesson said?
hint: Each PostgreSQL connection is a process with memory of its own.

choices.text: Put a pool such as RDS Proxy in front, so they share a few dozen connections
choices.why: Right. Fewer connections, not a bigger number.

choices.text: Raise `max_connections` to 5,000 in the parameter group
choices.why: Each connection costs memory; thousands of them starve the cache the queries need.

choices.text: Move to Multi-AZ, which doubles the connections
choices.why: The standby takes no connections; it only waits.

choices.text: Switch to MySQL, which has no limit
choices.why: Every engine has a connection limit.
